questions.stem: A 'multimodal' text:
options: can be read along more than one pathway, chosen by the reader
combines two or more modes, such as words, images, sound and movement
is delivered through a digital medium, such as a website, app or game
blends the conventions of two or more genres, such as memoir and satire
questions.explanation: Multimodal texts make meaning through several modes at once, such as written language, images, sound and movement. A text need not be digital to be multimodal, and blending genres or offering several pathways are hybridity and non-linearity, not multimodality.

questions.stem: Textual hybridity is:
options: the blending of different forms, genres or modes within one text
the reworking of an earlier text for a new context and a new audience
the extension of one story world across several separate media
the use of brief references to other texts within a single text
questions.explanation: A hybrid text mixes forms or genres within itself, such as a memoir combining prose, photographs and messages. Reworking an earlier text is appropriation, spreading a story world across media is transmedia storytelling, and brief references are allusions.

questions.stem: A memoir that mixes prose, photographs, text messages and hand-drawn maps is best described as:
options: an appropriated text
a hybrid text
a transmedia text
an interactive text
questions.explanation: Combining several forms and modes in one work makes it hybrid. Transmedia stories spread across several separate works, nothing here asks the reader to make choices, and the memoir is not reworking an earlier text.

questions.stem: A 'reading pathway' refers to:
options: the process by which a reader's context shapes their interpretation
the order in which a writer drafts and revises the parts of a text
the route a reader takes through a text, whether set or chosen
the sequence of events in a story, arranged from beginning to end
questions.explanation: Reading pathways describe how a reader or viewer moves through a text: line by line in print, or across links, panels and screens. The term is not the plot's sequence, the shaping of interpretation by context, or the writer's drafting process.

questions.stem: In a web documentary, viewers choose which interview to watch next from a map of locations. This interactivity most likely:
options: keeps a single fixed narrative, since the interviews are filmed in advance
gives audiences agency, so each viewer builds a different version of the story
removes the documentary maker's control over what the story includes
makes the documentary more objective, since viewers choose the evidence
questions.explanation: Interactive navigation lets viewers shape their own path, so experiences of the story differ. The maker still selects and shapes every interview, so control is shared rather than removed and the result is no more objective, and the order is not fixed.

questions.stem: On a news website's homepage, a large central image with a bold headline usually:
options: frames the main story as opinion rather than straight news reporting
creates a reading path that draws the eye to the main story first
gives each story equal weight so readers can choose their own path
signals the site's political bias by hiding the other stories
questions.explanation: Size, position and contrast make an element salient and guide where the eye goes first. The design ranks stories rather than giving them equal weight, it does not hide the others, and it says nothing about whether the story is opinion.

questions.stem: A story on a website uses hyperlinks that lead to characters' backstories. The hyperlinks mainly:
options: turn the story into a transmedia text spread across separate media
make the story hybrid by mixing fiction with factual background
create layered, branching pathways that readers choose to explore
fix a single linear pathway that readers must follow in order
questions.explanation: Hyperlinks create optional branches, so readers decide how deeply to explore. They do not impose one order, the story stays on one website rather than spreading across media, and characters' backstories are still fiction.

questions.stem: In a narrative video game, the player's choices decide which characters survive. Compared with a novel, this most clearly changes:
options: the audience's role, from observer to participant in shaping the outcome
the narrative point of view, from first person to an omniscient narrator
the story's genre, from literary fiction to fantasy or adventure
the role of the composer, who no longer shapes the possible outcomes
questions.explanation: Interactivity turns the audience into a co-creator of events, which a printed novel does not allow. The game's designers still write every possible outcome, and choice does not in itself change the point of view or the genre.

questions.stem: 'Choose your own adventure' books in print offered readers choices long before digital games. This shows that:
options: print texts offer more reader choice than digital texts can
interactive reading pathways are not exclusive to digital technology
print gamebooks were the first form of transmedia storytelling
digital games are adaptations of earlier choose-your-own-adventure books
questions.explanation: Branching gamebooks predate digital interactivity, so interactive pathways are not purely a digital invention. Gamebooks are single works rather than transmedia, digital games are not simply adaptations of them, and print does not offer more choice than digital forms.

questions.stem: In a graphic novel, a full-page panel appears after many small panels. This most likely:
options: speeds up the pace as the action builds
shifts the story into a flashback sequence
signals a change in the narrative point of view
creates emphasis and a pause at a key moment
questions.explanation: A large panel after small ones slows the reader and gives a moment visual weight. Runs of small panels tend to speed the pace instead, and a panel's size alone does not mark a flashback or a change of point of view.

questions.stem: A story is serialised in short instalments on a phone app. Each instalment is most likely to:
options: resolve its conflict so it can stand alone
recap the earlier events at length first
open slowly with long passages of setting
end on a hook to keep readers coming back
questions.explanation: Serial forms rely on cliffhangers and hooks to bring readers back for the next instalment. Resolving each conflict removes the reason to return, and long recaps or slow openings suit a short phone format poorly.

questions.stem: A podcast drama and a novel tell the same story. Which difference best illustrates how medium shapes meaning?
options: the novel was written first, so the podcast is an appropriation of the novel's ideas and plot
the podcast reaches a larger audience, because more people listen to podcasts than read novels
the podcast and novel share the same dialogue, so each scene's meaning stays the same in both
the podcast conveys a character's fear through breathing and silence, where the novel uses narration
questions.explanation: Each medium has its own resources: audio uses voice, breath and silence, while prose uses narration. Which version came first and how many people it reaches say nothing about how the medium makes meaning, and the same lines can mean differently when voiced.

questions.stem: A podcast drama is presented as a series of found audio recordings. This approach most likely creates:
options: distance, reminding listeners that the story is clearly invented
authenticity and gaps, as if listeners are uncovering evidence
an omniscient narrator who explains the events between recordings
a linear, continuous account told from one consistent perspective
questions.explanation: The found-recording device feels authentic and fragmentary, so listeners piece the story together. It works without an explaining narrator, the recordings come from different moments and voices, and it heightens rather than breaks the illusion of reality.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of telling a complex story in very short social media posts?
options: the form suits comic stories but is unable to carry serious ones
the form gives readers no way to respond to the story as it unfolds
nuance and inner life are hard to develop in brief fragments
the audience on social media is too small to follow a serial story
questions.explanation: Brevity makes depth and interiority harder to build, which is a genuine limitation of the form. Social media audiences are large, short forms can carry serious stories, and comments let readers respond as the story unfolds.

questions.stem: A writer of an interactive story finds that some readers miss the emotional climax by choosing a different path. This illustrates:
options: the death of the author, since readers now write the story's climax
a sign that the writer failed to plan the story's structure carefully
a limitation of non-linear forms, where control over meaning is shared
a strength of non-linear forms, which give each reader the same climax
questions.explanation: When readers choose their routes, the writer cannot guarantee they reach a key moment, which is a limitation of interactivity. Readers choose between paths the writer planned rather than writing the climax themselves, and the problem lies in the form rather than in poor planning.

questions.stem: A story is experienced on a phone at real locations around a city. This form mainly:
options: keeps fiction and reality apart by placing the story inside an app
turns the story into transmedia, since it moves across city sites
presents the city as a neutral backdrop with no bearing on meaning
links the narrative to physical place, blurring fiction and the reader's world
questions.explanation: Location-based storytelling ties events to actual places, so the reader's world becomes part of the fiction and the city shapes meaning. Moving between sites is not the same as moving across media, and the form merges rather than separates fiction and reality.

questions.stem: Transmedia storytelling is:
options: a single text that blends several modes, such as words, images and sound
a text that mixes the conventions of several genres in a single work
a story world extended across films, games and novels, each adding new parts
a story retold in a new medium, such as a novel adapted into a film
questions.explanation: Transmedia storytelling spreads a story world across several media, with each contributing new material. Retelling the same story in another medium is adaptation, and blending modes or genres within one text is multimodality or hybridity.

questions.stem: A trailer edits a film's scenes out of order over rising music. This mainly:
options: signals that the film itself uses a non-linear structure
summarises the plot so viewers can follow the film later
creates anticipation without revealing the full story
establishes the film's chronology for viewers in advance
questions.explanation: Trailers select and rearrange moments to intrigue without giving everything away. Out-of-order editing is a convention of trailers, so it neither sets out the chronology nor signals that the film itself is non-linear, and it avoids summarising the plot.

questions.stem: An online feature on a bushfire combines scrolling text, embedded video testimony, an animated map of the fire front and audio of a radio warning. Compared with a print article, the most significant difference in how meaning is made is that:
options: the video testimony replaces the written text as the main source of information
readers move through it in the same fixed linear order as in a print article
the animated map turns the factual report into a fictional, narrative-style account
the modes work together, so meaning comes from how text, image and sound combine
questions.explanation: In a multimodal text, meaning is built from the interplay of modes: the map shows spread, the testimony gives a human voice and the warning recreates urgency. The written text still contributes alongside the video, readers can move through the modes in different orders, and animation does not make a factual report fiction.

questions.stem: A web series about a high-school election is made to look like a political documentary, with talking-head interviews and on-screen captions. This hybrid of mockumentary and teen drama most likely:
options: appropriates one specific documentary so that viewers compare the two texts
invites viewers to read school politics as a satire of adult political spin
presents itself as a factual account of a real high-school election
uses documentary codes to make the teen drama more serious and less comic
questions.explanation: Borrowing documentary conventions for a school story creates an intertextual frame: viewers recognise the codes of political coverage and laugh at how seriously the students play the game. Mockumentary borrows the codes of a genre for comedy, rather than reworking one particular documentary or claiming the events are real.

questions.stem: A sitcom episode recreates a famous scene from a horror film. The joke depends on:
options: audiences recognising the original scene in its new comic context
the sitcom reproducing the horror film's mood of fear and suspense
the scene being an exact copy, so that no change in meaning occurs
audiences knowing the horror film's director and context of production
questions.explanation: Intertextual humour works when audiences recognise the source and enjoy the shift in context. The joke depends on the change in tone and meaning, not on recreating the fear, and viewers need to know the scene rather than the film's production history.

questions.stem: A pop music video reimagines a classic fairy tale with a heroine who rejects the prince. This appropriation most likely:
options: reshapes a familiar story to reflect contemporary values for a new audience
preserves the fairy tale's original values while updating its visual style
alludes briefly to the fairy tale without drawing on its plot or characters
parodies the fairy tale genre by exaggerating its romantic conventions
questions.explanation: Appropriations in popular culture rework familiar stories for new contexts and audiences, here updating the heroine's choices. The video changes the tale's values rather than preserving them, it reworks the whole story rather than alluding briefly to it, and rejecting the prince overturns rather than exaggerates the romance.

questions.stem: An animated children's film includes references to classic films that only adults will catch. These references mainly:
options: make the film an appropriation of the classic films it refers to
signal that the film's main audience is adults rather than children
make the film's plot depend on viewers knowing the earlier films
broaden the audience by offering different pleasures to children and adults
questions.explanation: Intertextuality affects audience: layered references let one film appeal to two groups at once. Passing references are allusions rather than a reworking of the earlier films, children remain the main audience, and the plot can be followed without catching them.

questions.stem: A public safety agency adapts a well-known children's story into a short animated advertisement about water safety. The adaptation mainly:
options: uses a familiar story to make a public message memorable
parodies the original story to mock its outdated values
alludes to the story in passing without adapting its plot
retells the story faithfully so its original meaning is kept
questions.explanation: Composers transform texts for new purposes, and a familiar narrative helps a message stick. The advertisement changes the story's purpose rather than keeping its original meaning, it adapts the characters and plot rather than just alluding to them, and nothing suggests mockery.

questions.stem: A political cartoon recreates a famous painting with politicians in place of the original figures. The intertextual link mainly serves to:
options: suggest the painting was originally a comment on modern politics
signal the cartoonist's admiration for the painting's style and artist
transfer the painting's associations to comment on the politicians
show respect for the painting by keeping its original meaning intact
questions.explanation: Borrowing a well-known image lets the cartoon draw on its meaning to make a point about the present. The purpose is political comment, not homage to the artist, preserving the painting's original meaning, or a claim about what the painting first meant.

questions.stem: Fan fiction that writes new adventures for characters from a popular series is an example of:
options: audiences becoming composers who extend and transform texts
transmedia storytelling planned by the series' original creators
an adaptation that retells the original story in a new medium
an allusion, since it refers briefly to an earlier popular text
questions.explanation: Fan fiction shows readers taking up the role of composer, appropriating characters and worlds for new stories. Transmedia extensions come from the creators themselves, adaptation retells the same story in a new medium, and fan fiction builds whole new stories rather than briefly alluding to the series.

questions.stem: A mash-up video combines scenes from two separate films to create a new story. This shows:
options: that remixing is a form of transmedia storytelling planned by studios
that a mash-up is a faithful adaptation of each of the original films
how digital tools let audiences remix existing texts into new meanings
that the original films' meanings carry over unchanged into the new story
questions.explanation: Remix culture uses accessible editing technology to recombine existing material into something new. The new context changes what the scenes mean, mash-ups are made by audiences rather than planned by studios, and they transform rather than faithfully adapt their sources.

questions.stem: A student argues that a short-form video series retelling a Shakespeare play 'trivialises' it. Which counter-argument best uses this focus area's ideas?
options: the new medium transforms the play for a new audience, bringing out different aspects of it
the series should be judged by how closely it reproduces the play's original language and plot
the series is popular with young viewers, which proves that it does justice to Shakespeare's play
Shakespeare's plays were popular entertainment in their own time, so any version of them has value
questions.explanation: The focus area considers how composers transform texts for new contexts, purposes and audiences, so an adaptation can be judged for what it reveals rather than for fidelity. Popularity is not evidence of value, and the play's original status does not make every version worthwhile.

questions.stem: A storytelling app shows the stories with the most 'likes' first. A critical reader might argue that this:
options: gives users full control, so the app's design carries no values of its own
ensures the most accurate and well-crafted stories reach the most readers
removes bias, since the ranking is calculated by an algorithm, not people
privileges popular, sensational stories and shapes which voices are heard
questions.explanation: Platforms carry values in their design, and ranking by popularity favours certain stories and voices. An algorithm still embodies its designers' choices, users do not control the ranking, and popularity is no guarantee of accuracy or craft.

questions.stem: Many video games make the player's character a lone hero who solves problems through combat. An assumption this may reflect is that:
options: conflict is best resolved by individual force
true heroism depends on cooperation within a team
stories need a group of equal protagonists
violence in games makes players aggressive
questions.explanation: Repeated patterns in a medium carry assumptions, and the combat-hero model implies that problems are solved by one person's force. Teamwork and shared heroism contradict the pattern, and a claim about games' effects on players is a debate about the medium, not an assumption the stories themselves embody.

questions.stem: A popular streaming series shows a diverse friendship group without making diversity the focus of its plot. This most likely reflects:
options: changing values that treat diversity as normal in mainstream storytelling
an assumption that diversity is a problem the story needs to resolve
an attempt to ignore diversity by leaving it out of the story's plot
a convention of television that dates back to its earliest decades
questions.explanation: Representing diversity as ordinary rather than as a problem to be resolved reflects shifting values. The group is diverse and on screen, so the series does not ignore it, and the pattern is recent rather than an early television convention.

questions.stem: A creator tells the story of a refugee's journey as an interactive game. A critic worries that the form may:
options: simplify the story, since game narratives lack characters and conflict
turn a true story into fiction, since games are a fictional form
turn real suffering into entertainment, though choice can also build empathy
make the refugee's story more accurate, since players make the choices
questions.explanation: Emerging forms raise questions about values: gameplay can trivialise trauma, yet making choices in a character's place can deepen empathy. Player choice does not make the story more accurate, games do use characters and conflict, and a game can represent real experience.

questions.stem: A fitness app presents each user's progress as a hero's journey, with levels titled 'The Call', 'The Ordeal' and 'Return Triumphant'. A critical reading of this narrative framing would most likely note that it:
options: subverts the hero's journey by denying users a final reward
presents fitness as a shared community effort with no central figure
casts self-improvement as a solitary quest that ends in certain triumph
keeps the narrative neutral, since level titles carry no values
questions.explanation: Emerging digital forms carry values through the narratives they borrow: the hero's-journey frame makes the user a lone hero and implies that effort guarantees success. The app follows the pattern through to triumph, keeps a single central figure, and its level titles are far from value-neutral.

questions.stem: In a reflection on composing a digital story, which sentence best reflects on the medium?
options: My story explores the theme of waiting, which many teenagers relate to.
I added a soundtrack to my digital story, which is about a girl waiting at a station.
The feedback from my classmates said that the story was very moving to watch.
I used a looping ambient soundtrack to suggest the character's endless waiting.
questions.explanation: Reflecting on composition in a medium means explaining how its particular resources served the purpose. Naming a soundtrack without its effect, stating a theme or reporting feedback does not reflect on the medium.

questions.stem: A student adapts her short story into a three-minute video. Which sentence from her reflection best shows how the change of medium changed her storytelling?
options: I chose a close-up for the opening because close-ups are a common film technique.
The video tells the same story as before, about a girl deciding whether to leave her town.
Without a narrator, I let a long close-up of her hands show the doubt the story described.
I kept the story's dialogue, so the video means exactly what the story meant.
questions.explanation: Reflecting on composing in a new medium means explaining how its resources replaced or changed the original's, here a close-up doing the work of narration. Keeping the dialogue, naming a technique without its purpose or summarising the plot says nothing about how the medium changed the storytelling.

questions.stem: A student turns a short story into a series of images with captions for social media. To keep the narrative clear she should most likely:
options: sequence the images so each caption advances the story and leads to the next
post the full story as text in the first caption, then add the images
choose striking images and keep the captions vague to build mystery
use one image per character so readers learn who everyone is first
questions.explanation: Experimenting with a new form means using its structures well: ordered images with linking captions create a readable sequence. Front-loading the story in text, vague captions or a gallery of characters all work against a clear narrative.

questions.stem: A student planning a digital narrative uses a storyboard. This mainly helps her:
options: edit the finished footage into its final order after production
plan the sequence of images, text and sound before production
draft the written script and dialogue for each of her characters
record the feedback her audience gives on the finished narrative
questions.explanation: A storyboard organises shots, text and sound in sequence so the composer can plan and refine before producing. A script holds the dialogue, editing happens after production, and audience feedback comes once the work is finished.

questions.stem: An essay on a multimodal text is most cohesive if each paragraph:
options: covers as many techniques as possible to show the text's full range
links a specific technique to a clear argument and connects to the next point
analyses a different mode of the text, such as its images or its sound
begins with a quotation and ends by summarising what the paragraph said
questions.explanation: The syllabus asks for logical, ordered and cohesive texts that build arguments, which requires each paragraph to argue and to link. Organising by mode, a fixed quotation-and-summary pattern or covering many techniques does not by itself build a connected argument.
